newsitem.title: JAPAN: Multinational meeting to push Siberia gas project.
newsitem.headline: Multinational meeting to push Siberia gas project.

text.p: Officials from Japan, South Korea, Russia and China will meet by the end of the year in Moscow to discuss joint development of potentially huge gas fields in Siberia, a Japan National Oil Co official said on Thursday.
"It will be the first time all four parties involved in the project will get together," the official told Reuters.

When Russian President Boris Yeltsin visited Beijing in April, Beijing and Moscow signed an energy cooperation package, including a multi-billion-dollar plan to build a pipeline to send natural gas from eastern Siberia to China, and possibly from there onto South Korea and Japan.
Eastern Siberia's huge untapped natural gas reserves have attracted attention partly because of their proximity to Asia's economic powerhouses, natural gas traders in Japan said.
The Moscow meeting is expected to look at how to carry out feasibility studies for the pipeline construction and exploration of the gas fields, the Japanese official said.
A pipeline route has not been decided, but one suggested course is from the gas-rich Irkutsk region near Lake Baikal, through Mongolia to the coast near the major city of Tianjin, traders said.
It would then go undersea from there to South Korea, one trader said.
There are many unanswered questions surrounding the project, including ones about possible starting dates and financing.

The estimated cost of the pipeline project ranges from $4.5 billion to as much as $14.4 billion if it is extended all the way to Kitakyushu in western Japan, Mikhail Surtsukov, an official from one of Russia's major oil companies Sidanco, told a seminar last month in Tokyo.
He also told the seminar that the Kovyktinskoye field in Irkutsk has 870 billion cubic metres (30.6 trillion cubic feet) of proven gas reserves.
Officials from the Russian Fuel and Energy Ministry are expected to attend the meeting as are representatives from the China National Petroleum Corp, traders said.
South Korea is expected to dispatch officials from its Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy as well as from the Korea Gas Corp, they said.
The Korean ministry said earlier this year that the Korean consortium for the project would be led by the state-run gas firm, and that six private companies would take part.
In addition to the semi-governmental Japan National Oil Co, major Japanese trading houses are also expected to attend the meeting.

The traders said Japan's involvement in the project would help provide it with a stable supply of natural gas, widely regarded as clean energy, while giving the Sino-Russian side much-needed financial support for the massive project.

It would also diversify energy sources for Japan, which now depends on the Middle Eastern countries for almost 80 percent of its crude oil, while 60 percent of its liquefied natural gas imports come from Indonesia and Malaysia.
